title: Al-Khwarizmi and the Birth of Algebra (9th century)
explainer: The idea of manipulating an unknown quantity by a fixed procedure traces back to the 9th-century mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose Baghdad treatise on solving equations gave Europe both the word 'algebra' (from 'al-jabr') and, through a Latin rendering of his name, the word 'algorithm.' His unknowns were still written out in words rather than symbols, a reminder that the mental concept of a variable is older and more basic than any particular notation for it, including the ones used in programming languages today.

title: Viète, Descartes, and the Letters x, y, z (16th-17th century)
explainer: Using letters as placeholders for numbers is a relatively recent invention: the French mathematician François Viète introduced systematic letter notation for knowns and unknowns around 1591, and René Descartes's 1637 'La Géométrie' popularized using letters from the end of the alphabet (x, y, z) for unknown quantities. Seeing that this notation had to be invented, and was argued over for decades, makes it easier to accept that a variable in code is just another human-made convention for 'a slot that holds a value,' not a fact about the universe.
